target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good because it improves convenience, reduces routine work, boosts accessibility, and improves safety.
objection: AI’s benefits are outweighed by harms: automation can replace jobs and lower workers’ bargaining power; AI can weaken critical thinking by substituting for human reasoning; it can reproduce and amplify racial bias; accessibility gains do not cancel system-wide unfairness and privacy intrusions; and safety features often require invasive data collection.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms are inevitable and that AI in general should be rejected because safeguards are assumed to fail.
objection: That conclusion assumes worst-case deployment and ignores that AI can be designed and governed in human-centered ways, with reskilling, augmentation, auditing, transparency, and privacy-preserving techniques that make the benefits real without treating harms as unavoidable.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s harms can be managed with governance, auditing, tutoring use, and privacy-preserving methods.
objection: In real-world deployment, incentives and practical constraints make safeguards unreliable, incomplete, or too slow. Business pressure favors rapid monetization over careful governance, so the risks remain systemic rather than hypothetical.

target: AG2’s claim that imperfect safeguards mean AI is not broadly good for society.
objection: The fact that safeguards are difficult is a risk-management problem, not a refutation. Society already regulates high-stakes technologies, and AI can likewise be deployed with standards, audits, and incident reporting to improve outcomes overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be made broadly beneficial through regulated deployment similar to other industries.
objection: AI differs from bounded industries like aviation or medicine because models are iterative, multi-purpose, and repurposed across changing contexts. That makes standards and incident reporting slower and less effective, especially when companies can update models without fully re-validating downstream uses.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up and therefore AI is not broadly good.
objection: Governance can still work through phased rollouts, continuous monitoring, scope limits, and required re-checks on meaningful model updates. The existence of risk is not a reason to reject all AI benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is good if benefits are targeted and governance is enforceable.
objection: If AI needs tight limits to avoid harm, it is not broadly good in a default sense, because most deployments will not actually meet those constraints. Competitive incentives create a race to deploy faster than regulators can validate.

target: AG2’s claim that net improvement is the wrong metric because harms remain somewhere.
objection: Good for society is about expected improvement, not perfection. AI can still make society better if it reduces injuries, improves accessibility, and supports learning for many people, even if some deployments are risky.

target: AG1’s claim that average net gains justify AI adoption.
objection: Average gains hide distributional harm: job insecurity, discrimination, learning erosion, and privacy loss fall disproportionately on workers, students, racial minorities, and ordinary users with less power to resist or recover from harms.

target: AG2’s claim that distributional harm and gateway risks defeat the case for AI.
objection: Those are reasons to evaluate outcomes by distribution, require independent re-approval for expansion, and use AI itself to improve governance. They do not show AI cannot be beneficial when properly constrained.

target: AG1’s claim that recourse, staged permissions, and AI-for-governance can make AI broadly good.
objection: Those solutions assume accountability systems that are weak in practice: people often lack meaningful recourse, staged permissions are not reliably enforced, and AI-based oversight can increase surveillance and bias while diffusing responsibility.

target: AG2’s claim that recourse and oversight are inherently ineffective.
objection: Recourse can be built through documented decision factors, audit logs, human review, procurement standards, and liability rules. Oversight can be privacy-minimizing rather than surveillance-heavy, so the harms are governance gaps, not proof that AI cannot be beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that procurement, liability, and privacy-minimizing telemetry can make AI broadly good.
objection: These mechanisms are structurally weak at scale: appeals are often paperwork without real power, procurement costs can concentrate good AI in wealthy institutions while others get worse tools, and telemetry still expands data collection and surveillance-like exposure.

target: AG2’s claim that AI cannot be broadly good because recourse, procurement, telemetry, and certification all fail in practice.
objection: Those risks can be addressed with human responsibility requirements, subsidized compliance, privacy-preserving monitoring, and continuous re-certification on model updates. The right response is stronger governance, not blanket rejection.

target: AG1’s claim that stronger governance solves the problem.
objection: The proposed safeguards still rely on heavy accountability systems that are difficult to enforce at scale. Logs may not create real remedies, continuous verification adds bureaucracy and privacy risk, procurement does not stop expansion incentives, and model drift undermines certifications.

target: AG2’s claim that governance mechanisms are too weak to justify AI as broadly good.
objection: Many AI uses are low-risk augmentation rather than high-stakes replacement, and the highest-risk uses can be restricted. Continuous monitoring can focus on system behavior, risk-tiering can be enforced, and AI can improve accountability rather than undermine it.

target: AG1’s claim that augmentative AI and risk-tiering make AI broadly good.
objection: Even augmentation can displace workers and increase managerial leverage; monitoring often still requires sensitive user data; products drift across risk categories; and automation bias means humans may defer to AI even when they are technically the final decision-makers.

target: AG2’s claim that augmentation, monitoring, and tiering failures defeat the case for AI.
objection: Automation bias can be mitigated by meaningful human-in-the-loop design, monitoring can use privacy-preserving methods, scope control can be technically enforced, and AI benefits can coexist with labor protections and workplace safety improvements.

target: AG1’s claim that better human-in-the-loop design, privacy-preserving monitoring, and technical scope controls make AI broadly good.
objection: Human-in-the-loop often becomes symbolic, monitoring still depends on sensitive feedback data, scope controls are bypassed through updates and repurposing, and affected people remain dependent on vendors who control the model and the remedies.

target: AG2’s claim that human-in-the-loop, monitoring, and scope control are only symbolic.
objection: Meaningful review can be made auditable, monitoring can use aggregated and privacy-preserving data, scope control can be enforced through signed versions and permissioned APIs, and AI can increase traceability compared with opaque manual processes.

target: AG1’s claim that auditable human review, privacy-minimizing oversight, and traceability create real accountability.
objection: Audits may still be rubber-stamping, privacy-minimizing oversight still requires collecting sensitive traces, locked versions do not prevent downstream context drift, and traceability often documents events without producing genuine remedies.

target: AG2’s claim that these governance tools cannot produce real accountability.
objection: The solution is to require decision authority, privacy-by-design evaluation, version control, and traceability tied to remedies. Governance can make AI beneficial without pretending every deployment will be perfect.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can make AI beneficial at scale.
objection: The needed accountability systems are structurally hard to sustain because authority is constrained by incentives, privacy-by-design still requires ongoing sensitive data feedback, explanations and logs do not reliably support due process, and compliance burdens fall hardest on vulnerable organizations and people.

target: AG2’s claim that structural problems make responsible AI impossible.
objection: Independent oversight, procurement rules, privacy-safe evaluation, standardized remedies, and subsidized compliance can convert responsible AI from a vendor promise into an enforceable public requirement. The existence of governance burdens is not proof that AI cannot be broadly good.
